note: Plain-language summaries placed at the top of the public Discussion threads (the product owner's request of 2026-11-09). About 120 words each, no decision numbers, hashes or file paths. The full record stays below the summary in the thread.

D236.decided: How the team picks which AI assistants do each job on a card, and what it does when one of them misbehaves.
D236.why: Assistants were being left out of the rotation for days because a status label said they were out of quota, or because they once gave an odd answer. The product owner asked that this stop: a label is a claim to check, and a misbehaving assistant should be fixed, not benched.
D236.changes: Before every plan the team now runs a quick live test of every assistant and writes the result down. An assistant that passes goes back into use at once. One that misbehaves gets its cause found and fixed, and the fix is written down.
D236.options: Keeping the old habit of routing around a problem assistant was the alternative; it hid the causes and wasted capacity.
D236.outcome: Adopted. Two reviewers first objected (they wanted proof a git check can verify); their conditions were built into the rule and they agreed.

D237.decided: The plan for card 162: teach the language guide and cheat sheet the two newest features, then re-run the test where AI models try to write Avowry from those two pages alone.
D237.why: The person who will write Avowry with an AI assistant only reads the guide and the cheat sheet. They did not yet explain the checking step or the copy-with-one-change step, so the earlier test no longer matched what people read.
D237.changes: The two pages gain short sections on both features. Two AI models then re-run the same test as before, so the results can be compared with the earlier ones.
D237.options: Splitting the work into two cards was considered; one card was chosen so the pages change only once.
D237.outcome: Adopted by six reviewers, with no objection.
D237.owner: Nothing needed. One model's half of the test waits until its usage allowance returns on 11 November.

D238.decided: Freezing the exact wording of the documents that the AI-writing test reads, once the team finishes editing them.
D238.why: The test only means something if every model reads exactly the same pages. If anyone changes a page while the test is running, the results cannot be compared.
D238.changes: The pages and test files are recorded as they now are. From now until card 162 finishes, no one may edit them, and an automatic check fails if a recorded page differs from its record.
D238.options: Relying on the team simply remembering not to edit was considered and rejected.
D238.outcome: Adopted. One reviewer first objected that the freeze depends on automatic checks rather than on the code storage system itself; the team pointed to the rule already adopted for this, and the reviewer withdrew the objection.

D239.decided: The plan for card 376: remove the machine owner's account name from every file in the public repository and make the scan that looks for it fail loudly.
D239.why: A public repository should not show the name of the account on the maintainer's computer. Earlier work removed it from file paths but it still stood alone in eight files, and the scan reported success even when it found something.
D239.changes: The name is replaced everywhere it appeared, the scan now stops with an error when it finds the name or a home path, and names made of two words are cleaned up completely.
D239.options: Rewriting the full git history was left out on purpose; that is a separate decision for the owner.
D239.outcome: Adopted by six reviewers, with no objection.
D239.owner: Optional: decide whether old history, which still contains the name, should be rewritten.

D240.decided: A new safeguard: before the team sends any text to an outside AI service, it checks that the text does not contain the account name of the machine.
D240.why: While reviewing card 376, a prompt carried the old account name to an outside service by accident. The team caught it by hand, after the fact.
D240.changes: For the next three cards, every launcher that sends text to an outside AI service refuses to send a text containing the name, and writes a line in a log so the check can be verified later. Until the tooling exists, the team checks by hand.
D240.options: Relying on people to remember was the alternative; five of seven team members judged that a practice is not a guard.
D240.outcome: Adopted. Two reviewers first objected; the safeguard was narrowed to the account name only and given a verifiable log, and both agreed.
D240.owner: For your information: the account name reached one outside AI vendor once, in that review. Nothing else is needed.

D241.decided: The plan for the work item called card 365: stop the team's own voting tool from rejecting several voters that start at the same moment.
D241.why: The tool keeps a log of who voted when that can only be added to, and it wrongly raised an error when two voters wrote to it at once. The team has run voters one at a time as a workaround, which makes each decision take 15 to 30 minutes instead of about 5.
D241.changes: Voters can start together again. Each write briefly holds back other writers; the log still cannot be edited after the fact, and any change would still show. A second card then fixes leftover scratch files that the same tool leaves behind.
D241.options: Separate files per voter merged at the end were considered; they would weaken the tamper-evidence.
D241.outcome: Adopted by six reviewers, with no objection.
D241.owner: Nothing needed. A later decision will remove the one-at-a-time workaround.

RETRO376.decided: Looking back on card 376, which removed the machine owner's account name from the public repository.
RETRO376.why: Each card ends with a short review of what worked, what did not, and what to change.
RETRO376.changes: One new safeguard was adopted (see the decision about checking text before it goes to outside AI services). Other ideas were noted for later.
RETRO376.options: Several ideas came up, such as marking in git which assistant wrote which change; only one was chosen at a time.
RETRO376.outcome: The card passed all its checks (743 tests, none failed). One slip is reported: the old account name reached one outside AI vendor in a review.
RETRO376.owner: You may want to decide whether to rewrite old history that still contains the name.

D242.decided: A new working rule for the AI assistants that write code for the team: when they edit a file, they must keep the file's existing line-ending style instead of converting it.
D242.why: On the voting-tool fix, an assistant was told to save every file the same way, so it rewrote a whole test file. The change then looked like every line had changed, which hid the real edit from reviewers. The team had to undo it by hand.
D242.changes: For the next three cards the instructions to writing assistants change, and a quick comparison of the change with and without line-ending differences flags any file that was converted, so it is put back before it is saved.
D242.options: Leaving the instruction as it was and fixing files by hand each time was the alternative; all seven reviewers named this as the one thing to fix.
D242.outcome: Adopted. Six reviewers agreed in the first round and six different reviewers agreed again in the second round the rules require for a change to the team agreement.

RETRO365.decided: Looking back on card 365, which fixed the team's voting tool so several voters can start at the same moment.
RETRO365.why: Each card ends with a short review of what worked, what did not, and what to change.
RETRO365.changes: One new working rule was adopted (keep a file's existing line-ending style). A card for the leftover scratch files is next; after that the one-voter-at-a-time workaround can be removed.
RETRO365.options: Several smaller ideas came up, such as checking an assistant's usage allowance before it is given a job; they were noted for later.
RETRO365.outcome: The fix passed all checks: the whole tooling test suite ran 1966 tests with only the five failures that already existed before this card. Six voters starting together now all succeed, and the log still refuses edits to earlier entries.
RETRO365.owner: Nothing needed. Decision time per vote window before the fix: 18 to 40 minutes; the after numbers come with the next windows.

D244.decided: Whether the team's decision votes may run all at the same time again, instead of one voter after another.
D244.why: Voters had to go one at a time since two bugs in the team's voting tool made simultaneous voters fail. That cost 15 to 30 minutes per decision instead of about 5. The product owner asked for it to be fixed and then switched back.
D244.changes: One sentence is removed from the team agreement (the rule that voters run one at a time while the two bugs are open). The safety rules stay: a fallback to one-at-a-time if the log cannot be written safely, and a check that no stray scratch files are lying around before a vote.
D244.options: Keeping the rule 'just in case' was considered; the evidence shows seven voters at once finished in 6 minutes 20 seconds with no voter refused.
D244.outcome: Adopted. Six reviewers agreed, and six different reviewers agreed again in the second round that a change to the agreement requires.
D244.owner: Nothing needed. Two smaller follow-up bugs are filed (hardening of the lock, and two other places that can still leave a scratch file).

D243.decided: A new check for the team's own process: before a quality test run starts, confirm that the code under test really contains the change being tested.
D243.why: On the last card a merge silently did not happen, so a 40-minute test run began on code without the fix. It was noticed after about 3 minutes, by luck.
D243.changes: For the next three cards the person running the tests writes down which version is being tested and proves it contains the change, and a refused merge is never hidden by cutting its output short.
D243.options: Relying on care alone was the alternative; six of seven team members named this check.
D243.outcome: Adopted. Six reviewers agreed in the first round and six different reviewers agreed again in the second round the rules require for a change to the team agreement. Both rounds ran with all voters at once and took under 5 minutes each.

RETRO374.decided: Looking back on card 374, which stopped the team's voting tool from leaving scratch files that made other simultaneous votes fail.
RETRO374.why: Each card ends with a short review of what worked, what did not, and what to change.
RETRO374.changes: One new check was proposed (verify that a merge landed before a test run starts). With card 365 and this card done, decisions run with all voters at once again.
RETRO374.options: Several ideas came up, such as fixing five older failing tests and checking the instructions given to the first-time Qwen writing assistant against the code.
RETRO374.outcome: The fix passed all checks: 1976 tests, with only the five failures that already existed. The retro itself, with seven voters at once, took 6 minutes 20 seconds.

D245.decided: A new rule for the team: when a change affects how an AI assistant is started, the team must start each affected assistant for real, in two kinds of folder, and keep the proof, before the change is accepted.
D245.why: On the last card, five faults in the new safety settings passed all automated tests and were found only when an assistant was actually started. Some made an assistant unable to run any command at all.
D245.changes: For the next three such cards, each affected assistant is started once in a plain folder and once in a project copy, runs one harmless command, and the proof (which version was tested and the exact output, with a checksum) is saved with the card. A small script will write that file so it cannot be typed by hand.
D245.options: Relying on the automated tests alone was the alternative; six of seven team members named a live start as the missing check.
D245.outcome: Adopted. One reviewer first objected that a hand-typed proof cannot be checked; the rule was changed so the proof carries the tested version and the exact output with a checksum and is written by a script, and the reviewer agreed.

RETRO379.decided: Looking back on card 379, which made the team's AI assistants unable to delete whole folders by accident.
RETRO379.why: Twice in two days an assistant typed a command that deletes a whole folder. Both times nothing was lost, but the ban only works if the tools enforce it.
RETRO379.changes: Assistants started through the team's tools now refuse folder-deleting commands: proved by running real assistants against folders that do not exist. One reviewed cleanup tool removes old throwaway copies, and only the facilitator runs it. One new rule was adopted (start each affected assistant for real before accepting such a change).
RETRO379.options: Several smaller ideas came up, such as asking a separate assistant to write the failing test when a live problem appears, instead of the facilitator.
RETRO379.outcome: The change passed all checks (2012 tests, only the five failures that already existed). It is not complete: three assistants (Muse, agy and Codex) are not covered yet, and your own interactive sessions get only a partial guard unless you install a setting on your machine.
RETRO379.owner: A decision for you: whether to install the guard in your own user-level Claude settings so it also covers interactive sessions and their helpers. It may also affect Cursor on this machine; say if you want that tried.

D246.decided: The team agreed the plan for its next product card: new benchmark result rows will no longer carry any part of the model's reply text.
D246.why: The benchmark history is public, and the owner does not want it to republish text that AI vendors' models wrote.
D246.changes: Both benchmark writers will stop saving the reply prefix, including the private holdout path and the per-model files. Rows already published stay exactly as they are, which a test proves with recorded checksums.
D246.options: None were contested; all six reviewers agreed.
D246.outcome: Adopted by six of six. Two reviewers had to be asked a second time because their first answer lacked a clear vote line.

D247.decided: A new rule for the team's test code: tests that start the benchmark tools under a strict time limit must run one class at a time, never alongside another such class.
D247.why: On the last card a timing test failed in two of four full test runs because other tests were starting the same tools at the same moment, which cost two sign-off attempts and about an hour of waiting.
D247.changes: Those test classes carry one shared label so the test runner never overlaps them. Until an automatic check exists, the independent reviewer checks every new class by hand; a bug filed now adds the automatic check, written failing first, and brings the two classes that still overlap into the group.
D247.options: Raising the time limit or leaving it as it is were the alternatives; six of seven reviewers wanted the classes serialised.
D247.outcome: Adopted for the next three cards. Five reviewers agreed outright. One reviewer first wanted the check automated, which was accepted, and still thinks three cards is too short a trial; that is recorded and the third retro will decide whether to extend it.

RETRO368.decided: Looking back on card 368, which stopped new benchmark result rows from carrying any part of the model's reply text.
RETRO368.why: The benchmark history is public and the owner did not want it to republish text written by AI vendors' models.
RETRO368.changes: Both benchmark writers, the private results path and the per-model files now save no reply text. The 336 and 120 rows already published are byte for byte unchanged, which a test proves. One new rule was adopted (the timing-test rule above).
RETRO368.options: Other ideas came up: one reviewed way to start background jobs (two were silently lost this card), a checklist of the tests that pin each documentation page, and a check on vote replies before they are counted.
RETRO368.outcome: Signed off on the second attempt (the first failed on a timing test that this card had made flakier). The final run passed all 344 and 402 tests.
RETRO368.owner: A decision for you: failed C# benchmark builds still save the temporary path, which includes the local account folder on Windows, in the row's diagnostics field. A bug is filed; it needs a rank.
